interactive.title: A measuring triangle on readings
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in twelve small screens. A graph has units on both axes: resistance R in ohms (Ω) up the side and temperature T in °C along, both starting at 0. Example readings of a motor winding sit as dots on a straight line that crosses the R axis well above the origin. A measuring triangle sits on the line; drag it along or stretch it by its corner. Its run is labelled in °C and its rise in Ω, and the readout divides the rise by the run, units and all, so the gradient shows in Ω per °C. It stays the same wherever the triangle sits and however big it is, because a straight line climbs the same amount for each 1 along. Where the line crosses the R axis a label reads 'R at 0 °C': T is 0 there, so the law's T part is 0 and only the intercept is left. The stretch of line below the first reading is dashed, because it is the line carried back past the readings, not a reading. Under the graph the law fills in, R = mT + c, with each number's unit beside it. Later screens show two windings' lines with a triangle on each, so you can see which sits higher and which climbs faster; a resistor's voltage against current, with a button that swaps the axes and flips the gradient's unit; a spring's force against its extension; and a lifting machine's effort against the load it lifts, where the intercept is the effort with no load on. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. A puzzle shows a graph and three answers. A wrong pick gets a one-line hint naming its slip, and Why? fills in the working.
interactive.ignores: The readings are example values, made up for the lesson, and they sit exactly on a line; real readings scatter a little around one, which the next lesson deals with. The dashed part back to 0 °C is a prediction from the line, not a measurement, and it holds only as far as the real law stays straight. The lifting machine's intercept is read from its graph; this lesson does not say what causes it. Real windings, resistors, springs and machines have their own figures.

explain.text:
When readings from a test fall on a straight line, the line's rule is a [[law]] for what you measured, and its two numbers are real quantities with units. The gradient is how fast one quantity changes with the other, and the intercept is how much there is when the other is 0. In many materials, how strongly the material resists current changes with temperature in approximately a straight line.[^1] So take an example motor winding read at 20, 40, 60 and 80 °C, giving 10.8, 11.6, 12.4 and 13.2 Ω. These made-up readings sit exactly on a line, an ideal case; real readings scatter a little, and laying a line through them is the next lesson.

Put a step triangle on the line from 20 °C to 60 °C. Its run is 40 °C and its rise is 1.6 Ω, so the gradient is 1.6 Ω ÷ 40 °C = 0.04 Ω per °C.[^2] The rise is in ohms and the run in degrees, so dividing one by the other gives ohms per degree: a gradient's unit is y's unit per x's unit. Stretch the triangle to 80 °C and the run is 60 °C and the rise 2.4 Ω, still 0.04 Ω per °C, because a straight line climbs the same amount for each 1 along. So the winding gains 0.04 Ω for every degree it warms.

The intercept is the value of R where the line crosses the R axis,[^3] where T is 0. In R = 0.04T + c the 0.04T part is 0 there, which leaves c, so c is R at 0 °C, in ohms. Carry the line back 20 °C from the first reading: 10.8 − 0.04 × 20 = 10.0 Ω. The law is R = 0.04T + 10. Physics writes such a law as R = R₀ + R₀αT, where R₀ is the resistance at the starting temperature, here 0 °C, and α is the temperature coefficient of the material.[^9] So the intercept is R₀ and the gradient is R₀α, and for these example readings α = gradient ÷ intercept = 0.04 ÷ 10 = 0.004 per °C, a figure worked out here, not a real winding's. 0 °C lies below the readings, so the 10 Ω trusts the line to stay straight down there. Engineering syllabuses and workbooks write the same law as y = ax + b, with a the gradient and b the intercept.[^4][^5] Each reading's ohms include that 10 Ω, so one reading divided by its temperature is not the gradient: 10.8 Ω ÷ 20 °C = 0.54 and 13.2 Ω ÷ 80 °C = 0.165, a different answer at each reading. That shortcut works only for a line through the origin, where c is 0. Use the law both ways: at 50 °C, R = 0.04 × 50 + 10 = 12.0 Ω, and a reading of 12.8 Ω means 12.8 − 10 = 0.04T, so T = 2.8 ÷ 0.04 = 70 °C.

Height and steepness are different things. A winding with R = 0.02T + 12 sits above one with R = 0.05T + 8 everywhere from 0 to 100 °C, yet the lower one gains 0.05 Ω for each degree, 2.5 times as fast. The same reading works on other laws. Plot a resistor's voltage up the side against its current along, and the gradient is its resistance,[^6] in volts per amp.[^7] Example readings of 6 V at 0.5 A and 24 V at 2 A give 18 V ÷ 1.5 A = 12 Ω. Swap the axes, current up the side, and the gradient flips to 1.5 A ÷ 18 V, about 0.083 A per V, which is not the resistance, so read the axis labels before you name a gradient. With force up the side and a spring's extension along, the straight part's gradient gives the spring constant,[^8] the force for each millimetre of stretch: say 10 N at 4 mm and 30 N at 12 mm give 20 N ÷ 8 mm = 2.5 N per mm. **A straight-line law's gradient is how fast y changes with x, in y's unit per x's unit, and its intercept is the value of y when x is 0, in y's unit.[^5]**

analogy.text: For one billing period, an electricity bill against the units used is a straight-line law. The standing charge is the intercept, the pounds you pay with no units used, and the unit rate is the gradient, in pounds per kWh: pounds up the side and kWh along give a gradient in y's unit per x's unit, as ohms and degrees give Ω per °C.
analogy.breaks: A tariff is set before you use anything, so you know its two numbers in advance; with a winding you have only the readings and work the law out from them. And the tariff's line is exact for any number of units, while the winding's line is approximate and trusted only near the temperatures it was read over.

practice.text:
- Read the axis labels first: which quantity is up the side, and in what unit.
- Pick two points on the line far apart and draw the step triangle between them.
- Gradient = rise ÷ run, dividing the units too: y's unit per x's unit.
- Intercept: the value of y at x = 0. If 0 is off the graph, work it out from a point as y − gradient × x.
- Write the law, then say each number in words with its unit.
- Check it with a reading you did not use.

**Rule of thumb:** the gradient is how fast, per one of x; the intercept is how much when x is 0.

**Worked example:** say a winding reads 4.5 Ω at 25 °C and 5.5 Ω at 75 °C. Gradient = (5.5 − 4.5) Ω ÷ (75 − 25) °C = 1.0 ÷ 50 = 0.02 Ω per °C. R at 0 °C = 4.5 − 0.02 × 25 = 4.0 Ω. So R = 0.02T + 4.0: the winding would read 4.0 Ω at 0 °C and gains 0.02 Ω for each degree. Check at 75 °C: 0.02 × 75 + 4.0 = 5.5 Ω. At 40 °C it would read 0.02 × 40 + 4.0 = 4.8 Ω.

**Common mistakes**
- Dividing one reading by its x. 5.5 Ω ÷ 75 °C is about 0.073, not 0.02, because the reading includes the 4.0 Ω at 0 °C.
- Taking the higher line as the steeper one. R = 0.02T + 12 sits above R = 0.05T + 8 from 0 to 100 °C but climbs less than half as fast.
- Turning the gradient upside down. 50 °C per Ω is the line read with the axes swapped, not its gradient in Ω per °C.
- Naming the gradient without reading the axes. With current up the side, a resistor's gradient is in amps per volt, and its resistance is 1 ÷ gradient.
- Using the first reading as the intercept. 4.5 Ω is R at 25 °C, not at 0 °C.

interactive.html:
Graphs with units on both axes, where example readings lie on straight lines and a step triangle measures each line.

Made-up example readings that sit exactly on their lines; a faint ring marks what you can drag.
interactive.title: A measuring triangle on readings
interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is the triangle's run in °C and rise in Ω changing together, so the gradient stays 0.04 Ω per °C, when you drag and stretch it along the readings' line.

checks.label: Wherever the measuring triangle sits on the winding's line and however far it is stretched, its run in °C and its rise in Ω change together and the gradient stays 0.04 Ω per °C

To find the gradient of a line joining two points, divide the difference in the y-coordinates by the difference in the x-coordinates: every step triangle drawn runs between two points on its line, its run is their difference along and its rise their difference up, and each gradient row divides that rise by that run

The y coordinate at the point where the line crosses the y axis is called the intercept, and in y = mx + c, c is the intercept: on every screen that finds it, the ring labelled with that value sits where the line, carried back, crosses the upright axis, and the law is written with it as c

In many materials the dependence of resistance on temperature is approximately linear and can be modelled using a linear equation: every example winding reading drawn sits on its winding's straight line, which runs solid from the first reading to the last

A plot of the voltage versus the current is approximately linear, and the slope of the line is the resistance, the voltage divided by the current: with voltage up the side, each example reading's voltage divided by its current equals the gradient, in volts per amp

The units of resistance are volts per ampere: the gradient is named as the resistance only with volts up the side; with the axes swapped it is in amps per volt, and the working says it is not the resistance

The gradient of the graph of force (y-axis) and extension (x-axis) is numerically equal to the spring constant: on the spring screen force is up the side, extension along, and the gradient comes out in newtons per millimetre

In the linear function f(x) = ax + b, a is the gradient and b is the vertical intercept: on the lifting machine screen a is the step triangle's rise over its run, b is where the line meets the effort axis, and the law is written with both
Every worked row is right, by hand: 2.4 Ω ÷ 60 °C = 0.04 Ω per °C, 10.8 − 0.04 × 20 = 10.0 Ω, 12.8 Ω means 70 °C, 18 V ÷ 1.5 A = 12 Ω, 1.5 A ÷ 18 V ≈ 0.083 A per V, and every puzzle's working

Before an answer a puzzle keeps back its working, triangles, intercept and guides; a right answer or Why? draws them; each wrong pick has a hint of its own, and a slip that can be drawn is drawn dashed

Every answer offered is written from its own numbers; the right one is worked from the puzzle's own readings, and each wrong one is a real slip: run over rise, one reading divided by its own x, a reading taken as the intercept, the step back added instead of taken away, the reading put in for the wrong letter, the intercept not taken away, height taken for steepness, the gradient named as the resistance, or the units turned round

Height and steepness are different things: A sits above B, and C above D, all the way along their graphs, yet over the same run the lower line's triangle rises further, wherever the triangles are dragged

The demonstration rests with voltage up the side; pressing Swap the axes carries each reading from its place with current along to its place with voltage along, and turns the gradient upside down, from volts per amp to amps per volt
The line is solid only between the first and last readings; carried back towards 0, or on past the readings, it is dashed, and a key in the drawing says what the dashes mean
Read both ways, the law's guides land where its rule says: up from 50 °C and across to 12.0 Ω, across from 12.8 Ω and down to 70 °C, and across from 13.6 Ω and down to 90 °C
Every demonstration has finished arriving within its 2.8 to 5 s, none starting before the 0.35 s screen fade ends; a puzzle's drawing finishes within 2.5 s

applied.problem: The spring gradient is the spring constant only while extension stays in proportion to force (the source's limit of proportionality); HELM [^5] is a workbook, not a syllabus; and the spring readings are made up but not worded as chosen.

The worked example's winding figures are assumed values (0.02 Ω per °C is not copper's figure) but read as a real winding; and 'the line meets it' points at the temperature axis, which the line does not meet at R at 20 °C.
